blocks.text: It has been proved so far that for most of the ancients סיס sis is the swallow. Against them Jonathan is cited in vain, as though he had rendered it כורכיא, that is, crane. For he correctly explained the two words סיס sis and עגור agor by כורכיא kurkeja and סנוניתא sununitha, that is, crane and swallow. For as סיס sis is the swallow, so עגור agor is the crane, as will be shown in the following chapter. But he inverted the order, and put the swallow, which comes first in the Hebrew text, in the second place. This often happens with translators. And, not to seek examples further afield, in the passage of Baruch which we cited a little earlier, for the Greek words νυκτερίδες, χελιδόνες [nykterides, chelidones], bats and swallows, the Arabic has, in inverted order, السنونو والوطاويط [al-sunūnū wa-l-waṭāwīṭ] swallows and bats. Accordingly we add the Chaldee also, whom the Syriac followed, to those of the ancients for whom סיס sis is the swallow. Thus there is now none of the early translators who does not agree with the rendering we maintain.

To this authority of the ancients is added a clear reason. The word סיס sis is ὀνοματοποιητικὴ [onomatopoiētikē], by which the Hebrew intended to imitate, after a fashion, the swallow's ψιθυρισμὸν [psithyrismon]. So with the Italians around Venice, for whom zisilla is the swallow, and zisillare means to τιτυβίζειν [titybizein] or ψιθυρίζειν [psithyrizein] in the manner of a swallow. The author of the Philomela said zinzilulare:
The wren and the bee-eater, and Procne with red breast, Know how to zinzilulare with a like measure.

As though the voice of Procne, that is, of the swallow, were zizi, from which zizilulare ought to have been said, as in Italian zisillare. But for the sake of euphony an epenthetic N was added, which is frequent in Roman words. Such are lingo from λείχω [leichō], linquo from the Aeolic λείκω [leikō] for λείπω [leipō], tango from θίγω [thigō], pango from πάγω [pagō] for πήγω [pēgō], densus from δασὺς [dasys], pinguis from παχὺς [pachys], etc. ^{(4)}.

Nor is it of slight weight that the Egyptians relate in their fables that Isis was changed into a swallow. Plutarch in the Isis: Αὐτὴν δὲ γενομένην χελιδόνα (φασὶ) [Autēn de genomenēn chelidona (phasi)]

[II, 606] τῇ κίονι περιπέτεσθαι, καὶ θρηνεῖν· [tē kioni peripetesthai, kai thrēnein] And she, having become a swallow (they say), flew around the pillar and lamented. For Isis plainly alludes to sis. And the fabulous metamorphoses of the gods often rest on allusions of words. Thus Anubis was represented with a dog's head, because in Hebrew נובח nobeah means barking. And king Apis was worshipped in a bull, because of the allusion to אביר abir: for the Hebrews so name the bull. Hence the LXX at Ier. XLVI, 15: Διὰ τί ἔφυγεν ὁ Ἄπις [Dia ti ephygen ho Apis], for the Hebrew [col. 63] מדוע נסחף אבירך, as they read in place of אביריך. And in the story of the Gigantomachy the gods, having taken flight into Egypt for fear of the giants, changed themselves into various forms. Ovid, book 5 of the Metamorphoses:

Jupiter, she said, became leader of the flock, whence even now Libyan Hammon is fashioned with curved horns: The Delian hid in a raven, the offspring of Semele in a goat, The sister of Phoebus in a cat, the daughter of Saturn in a snow-white cow, Venus in a fish, the Cyllenian in the wings of an ibis.
